newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia PM presses for independent blast inquiry.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia PM presses for independent blast inquiry.

text.p: Cambodian co-premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh called on Wednesday for an independent investigation of a deadly weekend grenade attack, saying he did not trust an interior ministry inquiry.

Adding to political pressure over the attack, which Ranariddh said killed 19 and wounded 119, the parliament's chief human rights official Kem Sokha urged the resignation of Cambodian government leaders.

"I would like the leaders of the government who committed the crime, who stand behind the crime, who helped plan the crime or who allowed this crime to happen to confess and resign their positions immediately," Kem Sokha said in a statement.
Asked who should resign, Kem Sokha would not elaborate.
The attack on Sunday occurred at a demonstration outside parliament led by opposition Khmer Nation Party President Sam Rainsy, who blamed the attack on his foe, co-premier Hun Sen.
Ranariddh and Hun Sen, whose Cambodian People's Party (CPP) rules the country in an uneasy coalition with the prince's FUNCINPEC party, agreed on Sunday on the ministry inquiry.

"As prime minister, I have to let the committee do its job but as a Cambodian citizen, I don't trust (it)," Ranariddh said. He wanted the independent body to be made up of Cambodians, but did not elaborate. Others have suggested it might include MPs.
Ranariddh, the Cambodia Office of the United Nations Centre for Human Rights (UNCHR) and Kem Sokha expressed doubts justice would be served by the ministry.

"I think there should be set up a politically neutral committee to investigate this unacceptable crime," Ranariddh told reporters after visiting the wounded in Phnom Penh's Calmette Hospital and handing out medicine, food and money.

The UNCHR backed the prince's call in a Wednesday statement, saying it "supports the creation of a truly independent, non-partisan commission to investigate this attack as thoroughly and expeditiously as possible".
It said consideration should be given to including internationally respected criminal investigators.
Kem Sokha, in a five-point statement, called for anyone in government who had been involved to quit.

He also urged the dismissal of corrupt judges and formation of an independent court, a parliamentary inquiry into the attack and the intervention of King Norodom Sihanouk and the international community to ensure justice was served.
Analysts said the authorities had failed to bring to justice those behind other incidents of politically motivated violence since the coalition was formed after U.N.-run polls in 1993.
Sam Rainsy, at a sombre cremation service under tight security for five attack victims, vowed to continue fighting for democracy and human rights despite Sunday's violence.
"Other people -- many other people -- are prepared to sacrifice their lives until justice prevails in Cambodia," he told mourners, who included family members and diplomats.
Ranariddh said the tragedy was a major setback for democracy in Cambodia, and reiterated: "It was not an isolated incident. I think it was a very well planned assassination attempt."
He told Reuters on Tuesday he feared the attack marked the onset of further violence ahead of the 1998 elections, in which Ranariddh's and Hun Sen's parties are set to oppose each other.
Ranariddh said it would become "more and more difficult" for the two leaders to work together as the polls approached.
